result.summary: Apollodorus lists the children of Zeus by Hera and by many other women and goddesses, including the Seasons, Fates, Graces and Muses. He then tells of the Muses' children (Linus, Orpheus, Hyacinth, Rhesus), the fall of Hephaestus, and the swallowing of Metis and birth of Athena.

scenes.title: Children of Zeus
scenes.summary: Zeus weds Hera and has children by many women, including Themis, Dione, Eurynome, Styx and Memory.

scenes.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
scenes.summary: Calliope's son Orpheus goes to Hades for Eurydice, loses her by looking back, and is later torn apart by the Maenads.
scenes.stakes: Orpheus risks losing his wife Eurydice forever; he loses her by disobeying the condition.

scenes.title: Hyacinth and Thamyris
scenes.summary: Clio bears Hyacinth, loved by Thamyris and Apollo; Thamyris challenges the Muses and is blinded.
scenes.stakes: Thamyris wagers his sight and minstrelsy against the Muses and loses both.

scenes.title: Other Children of the Muses
scenes.summary: Euterpe, Thalia and Melpomene bear Rhesus, the Corybantes and the Sirens.

scenes.title: Hephaestus Cast Out
scenes.summary: Hephaestus is thrown from heaven for helping Hera when Zeus hung her up, falls on Lemnos and is lamed.
scenes.stakes: Hephaestus is cast out and lamed for aiding Hera.

scenes.title: Birth of Athena
scenes.summary: Zeus swallows Metis to prevent a son overthrowing him; Athena springs armed from his head.
scenes.stakes: Zeus fears losing rule of heaven to a son of Metis.

alias_notes.explanation: Greek name of Memory, given in parentheses.

notable_quotes.reason: Introduces Orpheus, whose songs moved stones and trees.
Famous account of Athena leaping fully armed from Zeus's head.

analysis.text: The passage is a genealogy of Zeus's offspring, ordering divine society into Seasons, Fates, Graces and Muses.
Apollodorus gathers competing versions, noting variants such as Homer's, reflecting a scholarly effort to reconcile many Greek traditions.

legacy.text: The Orpheus and Eurydice story became a lasting subject of opera, poetry and art, from Monteverdi onward.
The birth of Athena from Zeus's head became a staple image in Greek vase painting and sculpture.

fun_facts.text: The Library is attributed to Apollodorus but was likely written in the first or second century AD.

language_notes.text: "Begat" is an archaic past tense of "beget", meaning to father a child.
"To wit" means "namely"; it introduces the names of the daughters just mentioned.
"Being fain to" means being eager or willing to; Orpheus wanted to bring Eurydice back up.
"Twitted" means teased or taunted; Clio mocked Aphrodite for loving Adonis.
"Quoit" is a heavy disc or ring thrown in games, like a discus; "involuntarily" means by accident.
"Bereft" means deprived; the loser would lose whatever the Muses chose to take.
"Lamed of his legs" means crippled in his legs.
"Taking time by the forelock" is an idiom for seizing the moment and acting at once.

context_notes.text: Orpheus was the legendary musician of Thrace; his father is given as Oeagrus, though Apollo is named as nominal father.
The Maenads were frenzied female followers of Dionysus, known for tearing living creatures apart.
The Sirens were creatures whose singing lured sailors to destruction; Ulysses later encounters them.
Athena, goddess of wisdom and war, is born from Zeus's head in this famous myth.

literary_notes.text: Orpheus's great music wins Eurydice back, yet one failure to obey undoes it; the brief sentence delivers the loss abruptly.
Thamyris loses his eyes and his minstrelsy, the very gifts he boasted of, as punishment for his pride.
Zeus's fear of a son who would overthrow him echoes his own overthrow of Cronus, and hints at Athena's unusual birth.
